item.title: Sudan Conflict and Complex Emergency- Public Health Situation Analysis (PHSA)
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Sudan’s war has shattered the country and shows little sign of abating, with the crisis driven by prolonged conflict, widespread displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks, and the collapse of essential services. Despite some progress in the first half of the year, including reduced overall displacement and modest gains in food security indicators, Sudan’s humanitarian situation remains extremely severe.

An estimated 19.5 million people, approximately 41% of the population, are currently experiencing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels of acute food insecurity. Without immediate action to reverse the current trajectory, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825 000. Anticipated El Niño-related climate shocks could worsen food insecurity and malnutrition and increase risks of cholera and other waterborne diseases, as well as malaria, Rift Valley fever and yellow fever.

Between 11 January and 15 October 2026, an estimated 119 782 individuals (23 598 households) were displaced from locations across Blue Nile state, placing further strain on health, protection and other essential services. Nearly 12 000 displaced people are sheltering in severely overcrowded schools with limited or no access to sanitation, electricity and other basic services.

The outlook is increasingly alarming as El Niño is driving severe drought conditions across more than half of Sudan, resulting in crop failures, water deficits, reduced agricultural recovery, declining incomes, and rising cereal prices.

Before the current conflict, Sudan had already been grappling with violence and displacement since the onset of the Darfur crisis in 2003. Sudan was home to more than 1 million refugees. Sudan has also been heavily impacted by severe weather events linked to climate change, including floods and droughts. These events have adversely affected hundreds of thousands of individuals throughout the country, leading to crop and livestock destruction and exacerbating food insecurity for families.

item.title: Syria: Protection and Reintegration Insights, Voices of returnees and host communities across Syria, July - September 2026
item.description:
Countries: Syrian Arab Republic, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Türkiye
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive Summary

Syria continues to experience significant population returns, with more than 1.8 million refugees and 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) having returned since December 2024. However, the pace of refugee returns has moderated throughout 2026, declining from over 268,000 in Q1 to approximately 131,000 in Q2 and 117,000 in Q3. Findings from the third quarter highlight persistent challenges affecting recovery and sustainable reintegration, particularly economic hardship, inadequate housing, gaps in civil documentation, limited access to essential services and localized protection risks.

This report draws on 9,842 household interviews conducted across all 14 governorates and 187 subdistricts, complemented by community consultations. Respondents comprised refugee returnees (45%), IDP returnees (29%) and host community members (26%). Building on three rounds of monitoring in 2026, the report identifies both improvements in selected indicators and persistent vulnerabilities, with variations across population groups and geographical areas.

Most surveyed returnees intend to remain in their current locations, although conditions for sustainable reintegration remain fragile. Among surveyed refugee and IDP returnees, 79% and 75%, respectively, reported intending to remain over the following six months. Improved security, family reunification and access to housing, land and property (HLP) were among the main reported factors influencing return decisions. However, damaged housing, limited infrastructure and services, livelihood constraints and security concerns remain important barriers to return. Phased returns, particularly among refugees returning from neighbouring countries, may also be linked to housing and livelihood constraints, although the monitoring does not establish the reasons for these arrangements.

Socioeconomic vulnerability remains a central concern, with important implications for protection and reintegration. Unemployment affected 31% of working-age respondents, rising to 36% among refugee returnees, with pronounced gender disparities. Food and nutrition remained the most frequently reported unmet need across population groups (65–73%), followed by economic opportunities. Financial pressures were also reflected in continued reliance on negative coping mechanisms, including depletion of savings (42%), deprioritization of essential needs (38%) and borrowing (26%). These findings point to persistent household vulnerability and associated protection risks.

Housing insecurity and unresolved HLP issues continue to affect households' living conditions and reintegration prospects. Refugee returnees reported higher unmet shelter needs (49%) than IDP returnees (35%) and host communities (19%). While most respondents expected to remain in their current accommodation, rental insecurity and affordability remained important concerns.

Gaps in civil documentation continue to restrict access to rights and essential services. Although modest improvements were recorded among returnees, 18% of refugee returnee households and 10% of IDP returnee households reported at least one member lacking essential documentation, compared with 6% among host communities. These findings reinforce the importance of accessible legal assistance and strengthened national civil registration systems.

Perceptions of safety and psychosocial well-being show some improvements, although localized protection concerns persist. In Q3, 87% of refugee returnees and 68% of host community respondents reported feeling safe, compared with 83% and 61% in Q2, respectively, while perceptions of safety among IDP returnees declined. Localized insecurity, movement restrictions and explosive ordnance contamination continued to pose protection risks. Reported stress-related symptoms also declined from 47% in Q1 to 38% in Q3, although economic hardship, insecurity and barriers to accessing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services remained important concerns.

Women and children continue to face distinct protection risks. Community consultations identified concerns related to gender-based violence, harassment, restrictions on women's and girls' freedom of movement and unequal access to resources. Child protection concerns included child labour, child marriage, violence, exploitation and exposure to explosive ordnance. Although reported school non-attendance declined among refugee returnee and host community households, economic pressures, child labour and documentation gaps continued to present barriers to education.

Social cohesion challenges remain localized but require continued attention, particularly in communities experiencing substantial returns and economic pressures. Community consultations identified tensions related to competition over resources, identity-based narratives and perceptions of unequal access to opportunities. Findings also point to the continued use of community-based dispute-resolution mechanisms, highlighting opportunities to strengthen inclusive dialogue and locally appropriate approaches to addressing disputes.

Access to humanitarian assistance has declined despite persistent needs. Only 29% of surveyed households reported receiving assistance in Q3, compared with 33% in Q2 and 45% in Q1. Among households reporting difficulties accessing assistance, service unavailability (64%), limited information (24%) and the absence of service providers (24%) were the most frequently cited barriers. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining assistance responsive to assessed vulnerabilities, particularly in underserved and high-return areas.

Overall, three rounds of protection monitoring in 2026 suggest that improvements in some safety, psychosocial, and education indicators have not yet translated into a corresponding reduction in the structural barriers affecting sustainable reintegration. Economic insecurity, housing and documentation challenges, uneven service availability and localized protection risks remain interconnected, with different implications for refugee returnees, IDP returnees and host communities.

Advancing durable solutions, including sustainable reintegration for those who have voluntarily returned, requires integrated, area-based and protection-sensitive approaches that connect humanitarian assistance with recovery and longer-term development efforts. Priorities include expanding access to livelihoods and essential services, supporting adequate housing and HLP rights, strengthening civil documentation and access to legal assistance, sustaining community-based psychosocial support, mitigating gender-based violence and child protection risks, and reinforcing explosive ordnance risk education and mine action.

Continued support to national and local institutions and coordinated service delivery are essential, with UNHCR contributing through protection monitoring, legal assistance, technical engagement, community consultations and coordination with government counterparts and relevant recovery and development actors. These efforts will be critical to creating the conditions necessary for safe, dignified and sustainable reintegration.

item.title: Ukraine: Returns to unsafe frontline areas: drivers of return and intentions to stay in Khersonska, Zaporizka and Sumska Oblasts, November 2026 [EN/UK]
item.description:
Country: Ukraine
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached files.

Introduction

Between June and July 2026, REACH in partnership with local NGOs Unity and Strength and Tenth of April conducted three assessments on unsafe returns (returns within 30 kilometres of the front line and/or the border with the Russian Federation) in Khersonska, Sumska and Zaporizka Oblasts. Interviewing 89 returnees with diverse displacement experiences (e.g., displaced abroad, displaced within the oblast), vulnerabilities (e.g., spent savings) and factors of resilience (e.g., owned housing), REACH examined what drove returnees away from “safer” locations, what pulled them to areas with ongoing insecurity, and their needs post-return.

Returns to unsafe areas remain a persistent concern for the humanitarian response in Ukraine. An estimated 4.2 million people had returned to their areas of origin or habitual residence as of May 2026. Returns to areas within 30 kilometres of the front line or the border accounted for roughly one-third of IDP returns since February 2022, an estimated 1.6 million people. The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan identifies returns to unsafe areas both as a protection risk and as a negative coping mechanism among people in prolonged displacement. The assessments aim to inform programming that 1) meets returnees’ specific needs in unsafe areas, and 2) improves conditions in areas of displacement to avoid returns made out of pressure rather than choice.

Across Khersonska, Sumska and Zaporizka Oblasts, respondents returned to frontline areas despite the (increased) insecurity – the initial trigger of their displacement. Most had left because of occupation, shelling or a specific attack; these threats remained at the time of interview, and respondents were aware of them when deciding to return. Some described insecurity in locations of displacement, such as Kyiv and Odesa, as equivalent to the security considerations that had triggered their displacement, while others felt the pressures (e.g., family separation) and vulnerabilities (e.g., spent savings) accrued in displacement eventually outweighed security conditions.

Economic pressure and relational and emotional factors appeared as key considerations in all three assessments. Return mostly followed a period in which displacement became difficult to sustain – due to rent, depleted savings, social isolation or family separation – rather than an improvement in security at home. These accounts indicate that negative experiences during displacement contributed to some respondents’ decisions to return despite continuing insecurity. Combined with ccess to owned housing, family, work or familiar services at home, respondents felt compelled to return despite the insecurity. Return reduced some pressures but did not resolve all needs. Some returnees struggled to recover from displacement even after return, for example due to accumulated home repairs or debt. As return at times prolonged or exacerbated vulnerabilities (rather than addressing them), continued insecurity may displace returnees again. Respondents’ intentions to stay were often conditional on security, housing and services. Households facing repeated displacement may be particularly vulnerable, as repeated moves are likely to erode coping capacities over time.

Differences in return decisions and post-return experiences were clearer between groups of respondents than between oblasts. Those who were older, displaced for shorter periods, displaced from occupied territories or displaced abroad were often flagged as particularly vulnerable post-return, while returnees to rural areas often had diverging experiences from those returning to urban areas.

This summary presents the key findings of REACH’s Unsafe Returns assessments. Oblastspecific information can be found in the Khersonska, Sumska and Zaporizka briefs.

item.title: Haiti: Haïti | Initiative Conjointe de Suivi des Marchés (ICSM) : Panier de Dépenses Minimales (MEB) Non Alimentaire et Estimation de la Valeur de Transfert (10 - 15 août 2026)
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached file.

RÉSULTATS CLÉS

• Lors du cycle d’août 2026, le coût du MEB multisectoriel non alimentaire était le plus élevé dans la ZMPAP, aussi bien pour le panier de crise prolongée que pour celui d’urgence. À l’inverse, le Nord-Est enregistrait les coûts les plus faibles pour les deux paniers. Ces disparités pourraient notamment refléter des différences dans les conditions d’approvisionnement et les coûts de transport.

• Aucun des 23 marchés évalués ne présente une fonctionnalité complète ou limitée : 15 présentent des problèmes sévères et 8 une fonctionnalité pauvre. Les principales faiblesses concernent l’abordabilité, la résilience des approvisionnements et les infrastructures, tandis que l’accessibilité physique et la disponibilité des produits obtiennent des résultats relativement plus favorables.

• Les difficultés d’approvisionnement varient selon les marchés évalués. Si 23% des vendeurs interrogés rapportent au moins une rupture de stock au cours du mois précédant l’enquête, cette proportion atteint 46% dans la ZMPAP et le NordOuest. Par ailleurs, les prix élevés des fournisseurs (41%) et le manque de fonds (33%) constituent les principales contraintes rapportées par les vendeurs pour maintenir leur approvisionnement.

item.title: Haiti: Haïti - Artibonite, Centre, Ouest : Suivi des Risques de Protection (SRP) - Août 2026
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Sources: Protection Cluster, REACH Initiative, UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Messages clés

• Les violences basées sur le genre (37/39 sections communales) ; les séparations familiales (30/39) ; et les attaques contre les civils et infrastructures civiles (29/39) sont les risques de protection les plus rapportés dans les sections communales évaluées.

• L’accès réduit à la nourriture ou aux marchés (35/39) et l’accès réduit ou interrompu aux services de base (33/39) ont été identifiés comme les impacts les plus fréquents des problèmes de protection au niveau des sections communales, tous problèmes confondus. Le problème de protection attaques et actes de violence contre la population semble contribuer particulièrement à cet accès réduit.

• Le problème de protection violences basées sur le genre a été directement rapporté par les IC dans la majorité des sections communales (27/39). Les filles et femmes sont les deux groupes rapporté le plus souvent comme vulnérables à ce problème (19/27 et 16/27, respectivement), bien que d’autres groupes (PDI, 8/27) ou tous les groupes sans distinction (9/27) ont également été rapportés comme vulnérables.

item.title: Syria: Humanitarian Situation Monitoring (HSM), November 2026 [EN/AR]
item.description:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached files.

KEY MESSAGES

• Livelihoods (68%) and food (66%) emerged as the two leading priority needs reported by KIs in assessed communities, largely driven by rising living costs. Nearly two-thirds of KIs (65%) reported substantial increases in living costs, while 94% of those reporting food-related difficulties cited the inability to afford food or associated fuel and transportation costs.

• Winterisation was the third most frequently reported priority need (53%), with rising heating fuel costs and inadequate electricity availability compounding seasonal vulnerabilities and increasing the risk that households will be forced to divert limited resources from food and other essential needs to maintain adequate warmth during winter.

• Rising fuel prices acted as a multi-sectoral crisis multiplier, driving up the costs of food, transportation, heating, agricultural production and essential services, with 92% of KIs identifying fuel price increases as a key driver of rising household costs.

• Deir-ez-Zor, Al-Hasakeh and Dar’a emerged as key areas of concern. In Deir-ez-Zor, livelihood deterioration and winterisation needs overlapped with food unaffordability and WASH and healthcare gaps; in Al-Hasakeh, severe food insecurity, winterisation pressures and limited access to essential services were compounded by declining purchasing power; while Dar’a faced overlapping water, shelter, livelihood and healthcare challenges.

Messages clés

item.title: Syria: Fuel Price Increases - Emerging Impacts and Outlook (November 2026)
item.description:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY MESSAGES

• Fuel price increases are reaching households mainly through higher transport and heating costs. Effects on other prices are so far limited: water trucking prices may be starting to rise, while food prices have remained relatively stable, indicating a need for close price monitoring.

• Rising transport costs are restricting households’ access to markets where essentials remain available. Increasing transport costs could particularly hit Al-Hasakeh and Ar-Raqqa, where around 40% of KIs reported that households rely on markets outside their community. Multi-purpose cash remains appropriate, except where markets may be facing shortages, such as fuel and core goods in As-Sweida.

• Fuel price increases are likely to further erode households’ living conditions as winter starts. Nearly half of KIs (47%) reported that households relied on purchased energy for heating. At October prices, the same amount of money buys about 30% less diesel than in August.

• In Al-Hasakeh and Deir-ez-Zor, fuel-dependent heating and water services coexist with widespread winter needs. As-Sweida faces the most acute price and supply pressures

item.title: Nepal: Rasuwa Flood Situation Report No. 13 (As of 20 November 2026)
item.description:
Country: Nepal
Sources: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, UN Resident Coordinator in Nepal

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • On 6 November, the National Planning Commission published the preliminary findings of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), estimating total damage and losses from the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi floods at NPR 472.66 billion (USD 3.18 billion) and recovery and reconstruction needs at NPR 706.65 billion (USD 4.76 billion).
  • According to the preliminary PDNA, the disaster resulted in 1,464 deaths, 5,285 people missing, and 13,795 people rescued, underscoring the scale of its human impact across affected districts.
  • CARE Nepal, Plan International, and UN Women released a joint Rapid Gender Analysis (RGA) of the flood response. The assessment found that women, children, persons with disabilities, and other marginalized groups face disproportionate recovery challenges, including livelihood loss, increased care burdens, psychosocial distress, and barriers to accessing services and decision-making, underscoring the need for gender-responsive and inclusive recovery support.

item.title: Briefing by Alexander De Croo, UNDP Administrator, to the UN Security Council on energy, needs and reconstruction efforts in Ukraine
item.description:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN Development Programme

As prepared for delivery

Mr. President, Members of the Security Council,

1. [Introduction]

Three hundred and seventy-two civilians killed.
Nearly two thousand injured.
Last month was the deadliest October since the full-scale invasion began.

And as winter approaches, the suffering is deepening.

Across Ukraine, repeated attacks are depriving civilians of heat, electricity, water and healthcare, services they need to survive.

Today, the front line extends far beyond the battlefield.

It runs through homes, hospitals, schools and businesses, and through the daily lives of millions of Ukrainians, victims of a war that is not of their own making.

The unprecedented scale with which Ukrainian energy and water grids have been attacked, can no longer be considered collateral damage. It is deliberately making life for ordinary citizens nearly impossible.

Air-raid sirens can sound at any hour.

Power cuts force hospitals to postpone procedures, schools to close and businesses to suspend operations. Disruptions to water and sanitation increase the risk to public health.

When I visited Ukraine in September, I saw this reality first-hand. I met people restoring essential services and rebuilding their communities while the war continued around them.

As one local partner told me: “We are not rebuilding after the war. We are rebuilding during the war.”

[Attacks on energy infrastructure and their impact on civilians]

Mr. President,

Last winter showed the scale of that challenge.

Ukraine’s energy infrastructure suffered damage on an unprecedented scale, leaving a gap of six gigawatts in generation capacity.

Extensive repairs helped stabilize the system over the summer.

But since mid-July, attacks have intensified. In some cases, energy facilities have been struck again before repair crews could finish their work.

Since October, attacks have increasingly targeted the high-voltage substations and transmission lines supplying major cities.

On 12 November alone, nearly 700,000 families were reportedly left without electricity.

For many Ukrainians, electricity can no longer be taken for granted.

People no longer count the hours without power. They count the precious hours when they have it.

This is far more than an infrastructure challenge.

It is a humanitarian challenge.
A development challenge.
And it is a direct threat to civilian resilience.

2. [UNDP’s support for emergency energy restoration and recovery]

UNDP is working with Ukraine’s national and local authorities to restore power today while supporting longer-term recovery.

This goes to the heart of our development mandate: keeping essential services running, protecting livelihoods and helping communities function.

We have supplied transformers to help restore the grid, and delivered generators and power stations to provide power locally.

Our energy support has reached 435 communities across all 24 regions. An estimated 6.7 million people benefit from improvements to energy, heating and water infrastructure.

In September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy and UNDP launched the Ukraine Energy Installation Facility to bring urgently needed energy equipment into service faster.

Our emergency energy support covers the full cycle, from design to installation and commissioning.

But repairing what was damaged is not enough. We are also helping Ukraine build a cleaner, more decentralized and resilient energy system through greater energy efficiency and passive protection for critical infrastructure.

Our objective is to restore the power and heat people need to survive this winter, while strengthening the energy system for the years ahead.

3. [Mine action]

Mr. President,

Mine action is fundamental to recovery.

Until land is safe, fields cannot be farmed, families cannot return home and communities cannot be rebuilt.

As we have heard from the World Food Programme, Ukraine’s ability to grow and ship food matters far beyond its borders. But food production begins with safe land.

UNDP supports the Government in surveying contaminated areas and prioritizing clearance.

To date, some 42,000 square kilometres of land have been returned to productive use.

4. [UNDP’s support for Ukraine’s wider recovery]

In war-damaged communities, making the land safe is only the beginning.

Debris must be cleared. Homes, schools and hospitals must be rebuilt. Public services must be restored. And people need livelihoods that allow them to return and rebuild their lives.

That is why UNDP works across the full recovery chain, from making communities safe to restoring the foundations of daily life.

With around 500 personnel working in Kyiv and six regional hubs, we support communities, including in front-line areas.

We help local authorities plan their recovery, repair homes and public buildings, equip health facilities and refurbish air-raid shelters, including in schools.

We help local businesses reopen, support young people and families returning home.

And make it easier for people to access public services online and through mobile teams.

Recovery must reach those who carry the scars of the battlefield.

That means helping veterans return to civilian life and supporting their families through that transition.

Local veterans’ centres bring rehabilitation, psychological support, legal advice, and training and employment services together under one roof.

Across, 13 oblasts, more than 1.3 million people benefit from UNDP-supported (local) recovery programmes.

Recovery also requires investment at scale.

UNDP’s technical assistance has also helped Ukraine unlock nearly US$1.6 billion in European Investment Bank financing to rebuild schools, hospitals and other essential infrastructure.

None of this would be possible without our donors. Their support keeps essential services running, helps communities rebuild and gives families hope for the future.

[Conclusion]

Mr. President, distinguished members of the Council,

Our responsibility is not only to help Ukrainians endure another winter.

It is to ensure that the support provided today lays the foundations for recovery tomorrow.

That is what development from day one means.

Ukraine is leading this effort, and UNDP is there to support it.

The people I met appreciate the UN presence and the work we are doing, but what they really need, is for this war to end.

And for this they look to you, Members of this Council, to help deliver it.

Thank you.
item.author: UN Development Programme

item.title: Ethiopia: Lethal artillery strikes on civilian neighbourhoods in Tigray’s Alamata city must be investigated as war crimes
item.description:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: Amnesty International

Please refer to the attached file.

Artillery attacks by Ethiopia’s military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm’s way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.

The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.

“For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants. The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes,” said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International’s Senior Director, Regional Human Rights Impact.

“For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants.

Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for Human Rights Impact

Amnesty International investigated four incidents of artillery shelling on Alamata by the ENDF and TPF between 26 and 28 September and independently verified the deaths of 14 civilians in these attacks. Researchers interviewed 28 individuals, including survivors, witnesses, relatives of victims, humanitarian and medical personnel. Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab analysed eight videos and 17 photographs, as well as satellite imagery of the site and other open-source information.

All names and identifying details have been withheld or changed to protect interviewees who requested anonymity.

Amnesty International wrote to the ENDF, TPF, and TPLF on 27 October, requesting information about these incidents. On 17 November, the organization shared its investigation findings with the ENDF and TPF and invited their comments. ENDF and TPF had not provided a response as at the time of publication.

The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes.

Yasmine Ahmed

In a four-page letter sent to Amnesty International on 18 November, the TPLF “categorically reject[ed]’’ the allegations made against it.

“While the preliminary findings acknowledge certain atrocities committed by the Ethiopian Federal Government and its forces we are deeply concerned by the allegations directed against the Tigray Security Forces [TPLF]. We categorically reject these allegations as unfounded and believe that they require further independent, impartial, and comprehensive investigation before any conclusions are drawn regarding responsibility’’ stated the letter sent by the TPLF.

Residential neighbourhoods at the mercy of ENDF and TPF Artillery shelling

Based on interviews with residents and two sources with direct knowledge of military movements during the offensive, Amnesty International identified Waja Ena Tumuga area as the main location from which ENDF and TPF forces shelled Alamata, approximately 13 kilometers south of the city. Two individuals with close knowledge of the TPF’s military capabilities told the organization that the TPF possessed artillery weaponry and participated alongside the ENDF in the operation to capture Alamata. One eyewitness saw ENDF forces moving their artillery into Waja, particularly the area that is called Ayer Marefiya.

Witnesses also told Amnesty International that the TPLF based themselves in and, in some instances, launched attacks from densely populated civilian areas in the city.

International humanitarian law requires all parties to a conflict to avoid, to the maximum extent feasible, placing military objectives within or near densely populated areas. They are also obliged to protect civilians from the effects of attacks by facilitating the evacuation of civilians from the vicinity of military objectives and giving effective warning of attacks that may affect the civilian population.

Any possible violation of international humanitarian law by TPLF through placing their forces and military objects inside densely populated neighbourhoods, does not absolve the ENDF and its allies of their obligations and can never justify the indiscriminate use of explosive weapons, such as artillery, in a densely populated area.

Yasmine Ahmed

Even though TPLF fighters possessed artillery capabilities and were actively launching artillery, it is highly unlikely that the shelling of Alamata was caused by direct shelling from their own forces within the city. While the possibility of technical failures cannot be fully dismissed, the likelihood of such a scenario is extremely low.

“Any possible violation of international humanitarian law by TPLF through placing their forces and military objects inside densely populated neighbourhoods, does not absolve the ENDF and its allies of their obligations and can never justify the indiscriminate use of explosive weapons, such as artillery, in a densely populated area,” said Yasmine Ahmed.

A medical worker, who was on duty in Alamata hospital between 26 and 28 September, told Amnesty International that almost all casualties recorded during those three days were civilians and that most of the injuries appeared to have been caused by shrapnel from explosive munitions.

Indiscriminate attacks on populated areas

One of the neighbourhoods most heavily hit by shelling was an area commonly known as the condominium area in Kebele 04, a densely populated area comprised mostly of houses and two multi-story buildings, which house hundreds of civilians and are adjacent to the single-family homes that were struck. Three eyewitnesses told Amnesty International that artillery struck five houses on 27 September at dawn, killing seven people and injuring four others.

Among those killed was Meron Sewasew, a 26-year-old mother of two, who died inside her home alongside her eight-year-old son, Markon Girmahiwot, and her older brother, Tewekel Sewasew, 33. Meron’s husband, Girmahiwot Negash [real name], said their two-year-old son was also in the house at the time of the attack but survived with minor injuries.

“I was away from the city for work. They were staying in the house because it was supposed to be safe from the war. She was my high school love, and our story ended too soon,” Girmahiwot said.

The same artillery attack also killed four members of a family living next door: Kumhis Kahsay, 40, and her 14-year-old child Helina Hailay, alongside Lezeu Yirga, 38, and her three-year old child.

I was away from the city for work. They were staying in the house because it was supposed to be safe from the war. She was my high school love, and our story ended too soon.

Girmahiwot

“Kumhis came from church that morning. All of the victims were outside the house doing chores. Kumhis, the older sister, was baking injera in the compound. I was inside the house. The remnants of the strike landed in the compound and struck them,” said a family member who survived the attack.

Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab verified four videos that showed damage to the two houses and one external structure within a compound located some 150 meters from Werknesh Hotel, a hotel which residents said had housed TPLF fighters.

“I saw TDF [TPLF] fighters on top of tall buildings with their weapons. They were telling us not to come closer. Some were staying at the Werknesh Hotel…. they were telling people to use a different route,” said an eyewitness who was in the area on 26 September.

Another individual who was near the hotel on the day of the attack told Amnesty International that TPLF fighters were not present near the hotel on the day of the strike. Amnesty International could not independently verify whether TPLF fighters were inside or near the hotel at the time. Three eyewitnesses said that minutes before artillery shells struck nearby residential homes, a separate strike fell just outside the hotel, causing significant damage to its exterior.

The ENDF and TPF also shelled areas where residents said there was no military presence.

On 26 September, artillery hit a local bar called Nigus Shimoy at around 11am, killing at least three people, according to a survivor who was injured in the attack and one witness. The bar is located at the entrance of a bustling market in a predominantly commercial area, bordering residential neighbourhoods. The attack took place as people came out en masse to celebrate Demera, the eve celebration of Meskel (Finding of the True Cross) holiday of the Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

I saw TDF [TPLF] fighters on top of tall buildings with their weapons. They were telling us not to come closer. Some were staying at the Werknesh Hotel…. they were telling people to use a different route.

Eyewitness

On 27 September, shelling hit a family home in another residential area, Kebele 02. Deyima Rebso, 55, was killed immediately in the attack in her home, while her husband, Ararse Yasin, 62, survived with severe injuries, according to an eyewitness. Their children, Saliha and Kedir, and grandchild, 10-year-old Sufiyan Abdulatif, also sustained serious injuries. Amnesty International’s weapons investigator identified munitions fragments recovered at the scene as consistent with an artillery round of the type fired by the ENDF and their allies.

One witness told Amnesty International that the house was the only structure to be struck in the area and that no military activity had been observed in the vicinity prior to the attack.

TPLF set up military bases in schools

Six people interviewed by Amnesty International said almost all schools in Alamata were used by TPLF fighters as military bases in the months before the outbreak of renewed hostilities. Witnesses said several schools, most of which were located close to civilian neighbourhoods, had been the site of military operations, including the launching of artillery shells after the renewed conflict began. All residents interviewed for this research said the TPLF didn’t issue any warnings or evacuation orders for residents near these locations.

On 26 September, an artillery shell struck a house in a highly populated neighbourhood known as Missionary Camp, near to Biruh Tesfa School, which had been used by the TPLF as a base. The attack, which occurred at around 6:45 pm, killed three civilians and injured four others. One witness said most of the fighters had left a week before the fighting broke out. Another saw a few fighters guarding the school in the days leading up to the strike.

Amnesty International could not independently confirm whether the school was ever attacked and whether or not the school was still harbouring fighters by the time of the strike. No damage or destruction was clearly visible in satellite imagery at the Biruh Tesfa school north of the charity compound.

A resident living near Alamata Preparatory School, another school, said that the school was targeted by an ENDF drone strike on 22 September. He said the school had been the main site from which TPLF launched artillery strikes to defend Alamata, until they began withdrawing from the city on 28 September.

“The explosion of weapons after it was hit by drone strikes affected the city, and we also saw some remnants fly by my house. There was artillery inside the school compound. We saw the weapons burning in the school that day,” said the resident.

Satellite imagery confirms a new burn scar became visible adjacent to the school on 22 September, aligning with the reports of a drone strike. Changes in vegetation were also detected around the school between 24 September and 1 October, though high-resolution imagery is not available to confirm the reason for the changes. Higher-resolution imagery from 21 October shows the clearing in more detail, along with a burned area within the trees.

False-colour, near infrared satellite imagery shows the preparatory school, highlighted with a white box. Healthy vegetation appears in red hues while recently burned areas appear black. On 19 September 2026, satellite imagery shows the vegetation surrounding the school appears healthy. On 23 September 2026, imagery shows a dark area within the vegetation – highlighted in yellow, suggesting the area was recently burned. Higher resolution imagery from 21 October 2026 confirms the area within the yellow circle appears burned

“Civilians are paying the ultimate price for the failure to hold perpetrators accountable in past and ongoing conflicts in Ethiopia. Impunity has emboldened perpetrators to carry on committing serious violations with no fear of the consequences. This must end. The UN Human Rights Council must act fast to establish an independent mechanism to investigate, identify those responsible for crimes under international law, and ensure they are held accountable,” said Yasmine Ahmed.

“Amnesty International also calls on the Ethiopian authorities to cooperate with independent international monitors, journalists, and humanitarian organizations to gain unhindered access to all conflict-impacted areas in the country.

Impunity has emboldened perpetrators to carry on committing serious violations with no fear of the consequences. This must end. The UN Human Rights Council must act fast to establish an independent mechanism to investigate, identify those responsible for crimes under international law, and ensure they are held accountable.

Yasmine Ahmed

“Considering the Ethiopian authorities’ persistent failure to ensure justice and accountability for crimes under international law, particularly where state forces themselves are alleged to have committed serious violations, urgent international scrutiny is needed. This is especially critical given the authorities’ record of suppressing independent human rights monitoring and the fact that Ethiopia is currently facing three ongoing armed conflicts, with growing risks of wider regional escalation’’ said Yasmine Ahmed.

Background

The armed conflict between the ENDF and its allies, including the TPF and other allied security and informal militia forces, and the TPLF and allies, including Amhara Fano forces and six other organized political and armed groups, erupted on 21 September 2026.

Fighting spread across three principal fronts initially: in southern Tigray, particularly the Raya Kobo Zone; western Afar (Zone 2); and the Wag Hemra Zone of the Amhara Region.

Since 21 September, the ENDF has carried out multiple aerial strikes in the southern Tigray, including in and around Alamata city.

item.title: Joint Statement on the International Court of Justice decision on Myanmar (23 November 2026)
item.description:
Country: Myanmar
Sources: Government of Australia, Government of Belgium, Government of Canada, Government of Cyprus, Government of Estonia, Government of Gambia, Government of Iceland, Government of Latvia, Government of Luxembourg, Government of New Zealand, Government of Portugal, Government of Spain, Government of the Czech Republic, Government of the United Kingdom

Joint statement with:

Foreign Ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia, United Kingdom

23 November 2026

We acknowledge the judgment of the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention).

The Court found that Myanmar violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention.

We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision.

This marks an important step toward accountability and justice for Rohingya victims and survivors, and for all those affected by the ongoing atrocities being committed in Myanmar.

The Rohingya have endured years of appalling violence, displacement and persecution. The Court’s ruling sends a clear message that such acts cannot be committed with impunity. Creating conditions for the voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar is essential.

We remain steadfast in our support for the victims and survivors of the atrocities committed against Rohingyas, and for all of the people of Myanmar and their pursuit of a peaceful, democratic and inclusive future.

Foreign Ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia, United Kingdom

item.title: South Sudan: UNMISS supports efforts to deter further violence in Tonj East following intercommunal clashes
item.description:
Country: South Sudan
Source: UN Mission in South Sudan

Please refer to the attached file.

JUBA - The United Nations Mission in South Sudan is engaging intensively with State, county, and local authorities to help de-escalate tensions and prevent further violence in Tonj East, Warrap State, following an armed attack on a cattle-camp and subsequent clashes over the weekend.

The mission has also deployed a peacekeeping patrol, which is en route to the affected area.

While casualty figures are yet to be verified, it is understood that there was a heavy death toll and many injuries suffered during the violent assault on the Bol-Bol cattle camp on 21 November 2026.

Families were also forced to flee their homes during the violence, leaving large numbers of people displaced.

After the initial incident, clashes reportedly continued in border areas between Tonj East County (Warrap State) and Mayendit County (Unity State).

The mission condemns this abhorrent attack on civilians and expresses its deepest condolences to the victims and their families. UNMISS urges authorities to strengthen security in the area to prevent retaliatory attacks, hold the perpetrators to account, and work closely with communities to reduce tensions, resolve grievances, and restore calm.

--
Contact: UNMISS Spokesperson at unmiss-spokesperson@un.org

item.title: Syria Polio Outbreak Response | Situation Report No. 1, 22 November 2026
item.description:
Countries: Syrian Arab Republic, Iraq
Sources: Government of the Syrian Arab Republic, UN Children's Fund, World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

In October 2026, after receiving initial reports of children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, Syria, the Ministry of Health (MoH) mounted a swift response, in coordination with partners.

Conflict, displacement, interrupted immunization and population movement have created immunity gaps. An unrelated variant VDPV1 detection was reported in wastewater in the area in February 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

The MoH, supported by WHO,UNICEF and partners, is leading the outbreak response, including intensified surveillance and vaccination.

Emergency vaccination activities reached:

  • 34 720 children in October 2026
  • 54 382 in November 2026 (111% of the target of 49 000)

The high coverage can be attributed to population movement. Additional efforts are needed to determine target population in future rounds.

The next campaign is planned for 30 November 2026 in six districts of Deir ez-Zor Governorate, integrating child nutrition assessments, drinking-water chlorine level checks and chlorine distribution.

An expanded scope will follow in December 2026.

The risk of further spread within Syria and to neighbouring countries, including Iraq, remains a concern due to uneven vaccination coverage and immunity gaps, particularly among displaced, mobile and underserved populations.

COORDINATION OF THE RESPONSE

The MoH is coordinating national and subnational actors. WHO and UNICEF are mobilizing regional and global technical expertise, while the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) provides technical and financial support. World Vision and the International Rescue Committee funded the first two vaccination rounds in October and November 2026.

Two coordination meetings involving national, regional and global response teams have reviewed the situation and agreed on priorities. The MoH Incident Management Team meets weekly through its Emergency Operations Centre. The remaining 13 governorates in Syria have been advised to intensify surveillance and preparedness. Cross-border coordination is particularly important for Iraq, given population movements and the history of wild poliovirus transmission across this border in 2013.

item.title: UNICEF Sudan Humanitarian Situation Report No. 47, 1-30 September 2026
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

  • In September, over 29,000 people were newly displaced, while more than 8.5 million remain internally displaced, placing immense pressure on basic services and humanitarian assistance.
  • UNICEF enabled 333,500 women and children to access primary healthcare, reached 144,200 people through emergency health services, and supported routine immunization, including 1.2 million children vaccinated with DTP1 and 919,000 with measles vaccine.
  • Nutrition interventions expanded, with 139,000 caregivers receiving IYCF counselling and 41,000 cartons of RUTF dispatched for severe acute malnutrition treatment.
  • UNICEF reached 7.7 million people with safe water services, 1.4 million children with education opportunities, and 184,784 children with psychosocial support.
  • As of 30 September 2026, only 40 per cent (US$382.5 million) of requirements had been secured, leaving a US$580.4 million funding gap, with critical shortfalls persisting in Child Protection, Nutrition, Health and humanitarian supply pipelines.

item.title: Malawi – District Profile: Chikwawa (October 2026)
item.description:
Country: Malawi
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

Under the Regional Response to Climate Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa (RE2CLID) program, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is implementing activities across eight districts in Malawi: Blantyre, Blantyre City, Chikwawa, Dowa, Mangochi, Mulanje, Nsanje and Phalombe. The district profiles bring together available data on population, climate hazards, displacement, vulnerability and local capacities in Chikwawa and will be complemented by the forthcoming RE2CLID Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) baseline assessment.

This profile is focused on Chikwawa District, which has experienced recurrent climate-related displacement associated with floods, tropical storms, cyclones and drought. The five Traditional Authorities (TAs) targeted by RE2CLID – Ngabu, Lundu, Makhwira, Maseya and Ngowe – were home to 348,079 people according to the 2018 Census, representing approximately 62 per cent of the district's population.

Historical DTM assessments show that these TAs also accounted for a high proportion of displacement recorded during major flood and storm events: approximately 94 per cent during the 2015 floods, 99 per cent during Cyclone Idai and 89 per cent following Cyclone Freddy. Patterns nevertheless varied between events. Displacement was concentrated particularly in TA Lundu during the 2015 floods and Cyclone Idai, while following Cyclone Freddy, DTM recorded 111,864 IDPs across 43 sites, with the largest shares located in TA Ngabu and TA Makhwira.

Looking ahead, the 2026/27 outlook points to a multi-hazard context. Under the DCCMS Strong El Niño scenario, Chikwawa is classified as extreme drought risk, while extreme-rainfall risk increases from no threat during October–December 2026 to extreme during January–March 2027. Understanding how historical displacement patterns intersect with current and projected climate risks can help inform anticipatory action, preparedness and targeted displacement monitoring.

item.title: World: Europe — Mixed Migration Flows to Europe, Quarterly Overview (July – September 2026)
item.description:
Countries: World, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta, Spain, Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

In late 2015, IOM launched a Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Flow Monitoring system, aiming to monitor Mixed Migration Flows to Europe by land and sea. Since then, DTM gathers, validates and disseminates information on migrants and refugees entering Europe through four main routes:

  • Eastern Mediterranean route (EMR): arrivals by sea and land to Bulgaria, Cyprus and Greece
  • Central Mediterranean route (CMR): arrivals by sea to Italy and Malta
  • Western Mediterranean route (WMR): arrivals by sea to the Peninsular Coasts of Spain, Balearic Islands, by land to the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla
  • Western African Atlantic route (WAAR): arrivals by sea to the Canary Islands of Spain

DTM also monitors data on migrants in transit through the Western Balkan route (WBR), including data from Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Kosovo (UNSCR 1244, 1999). These are considered separately to prevent, to the extent possible, the double counting of the same people, crossing multiple borders. Finally, DTM compiles data on migrants entering Croatia, Romania and Slovenia by land, typically after having crossed the Western Balkans or Bulgaria.

This report presents the latest available data and trends, focusing on the third quarter of 2026 and comparing it with the same period in 2025.

  • In the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), 36,097 migrants arrived in Europe via these four routes. This represents a 42 per cent increase from previous Q2 2026 and a 24 per cent decline compared with Q3 2025. The steepest year-on-year drop was on the CMR (down 59%), followed by the EMR (down 13%). Arrivals were distributed across the CMR to Italy and Malta (24%), the EMR to Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria (42%), the WMR to Spain (25%), and the WAAR to Spain (9%).
  • According to Eurostat, EU+ countries registered over 99,385 new asylum applications in the third quarter of 2026. Although data on asylum applications remain incomplete at the time of writing, France, Italy and Greece are among the highest ranking countries in the EU27+ in Q3 of 2026. Notably, France registered nearly twice as many first-time asylum applications (27,910) than Italy (15,450) did. Between July and September 2026, the main applicants held nationalities from Afghanistan (10%), Bangladesh (7%) and Sudan (6%), comprising nearly a quarter of all applications registered. These groups are followed by Türkiye, and Pakistan, Ukraine, Syrian Arab Republic and Somalia, averaging at around 4 per cent, respectively.
  • According to IOM’s MMP, 920 migrants died or went missing at sea while trying to reach Europe through the Mediterranean and Western African Atlantic routes in Q3 of 2026. Of these, 141 perished on the Central Mediterranean, and 350 while trying to cross the Atlantic to reach the Canary Islands. This represents a 6 per cent increase compared to Q3 2025 (871).
